title: Chapter 20 — That Aristocracy May Be Engendered By Manufactures
paragraphs: I have shown that democracy is favorable to the growth of manufactures and that it increases the numbers of the manufacturing classes without limit. We shall now see by what side road manufacturers may, in their turn, possibly bring men back to aristocracy. It is acknowledged that when a workman is engaged every day on the same detail, the whole commodity is produced with greater ease, speed, and economy. It is also acknowledged that the cost of producing manufactured goods is reduced by the size of the establishment in which they are made, and by the amount of capital employed or of credit. These truths had long been imperfectly understood, but in our time they have been demonstrated. They have already been applied to many very important kinds of manufacture, and the humblest will gradually be governed by them. I know of nothing in politics that deserves to fix the attention of the legislator more closely than these two new axioms of the science of manufactures.

When a workman is unceasingly and exclusively engaged in the making of one thing, he ultimately does his work with singular dexterity; but at the same time he loses the general faculty of applying his mind to the direction of the work. Each day he becomes more skillful and less industrious, so that it may be said of him that in proportion as the workman improves, the man is degraded. What can be expected of a man who has spent twenty years of his life making heads for pins? And to what can that mighty human intelligence, which has so often stirred the world, be applied in him, except to investigate the best method of making pinheads? When a workman has spent a considerable portion of his existence in this way, his thoughts are forever fixed on the object of his daily toil; his body has contracted certain fixed habits that it can never shake off. In a word, he no longer belongs to himself, but to the calling he has chosen. It is in vain that laws and manners have taken pains to level all barriers around such a man and to open to him on every side a thousand different paths to fortune; a theory of manufactures more powerful than manners and laws binds him to a craft, and often to a spot, which he cannot leave. It assigns him a certain place in society, beyond which he cannot go. In the midst of universal movement, it has made him stationary.

In proportion as the principle of the division of labor is more widely applied, the workman becomes weaker, more narrow-minded, and more dependent. The art advances, the artisan recedes. On the other hand, in proportion as it becomes clearer that manufactured products are cheaper and better the larger the manufacture and the more considerable the amount of capital employed, wealthy and educated men come forward to embark in manufactures previously abandoned to poor or ignorant craftsmen. The magnitude of the efforts required, and the importance of the results to be obtained, attract them. Thus at the very moment when the science of manufactures lowers the class of workmen, it raises the class of masters.

While the workman concentrates his faculties more and more on the study of a single detail, the master surveys a larger whole, and the mind of the latter is enlarged in proportion as that of the former is narrowed. Before long, the one will need nothing but physical strength without intelligence; the other will need science, and almost genius, to ensure success. This man resembles more and more the administrator of a vast empire—that man, a brute. Master and workman then have no similarity here, and their differences increase every day. They are only connected as the two rings at the ends of a long chain. Each of them fills the station made for him, and out of which he cannot climb: the one is continually, closely, and necessarily dependent on the other, and seems as much born to obey as the other is to command. What is this but aristocracy?

As the conditions of men composing the nation become more and more equal, the demand for manufactured commodities becomes more general and more extensive; and the cheapness that places these objects within the reach of slender fortunes becomes a great element of success. Hence every day there are more men of great wealth and education who devote their riches and knowledge to manufactures, and who seek, by opening large establishments and applying a strict division of labor, to meet the fresh demands coming in from all sides. Thus, in proportion as the mass of the nation turns to democracy, that particular class engaged in manufactures becomes more aristocratic. Men grow more alike in the one, more different in the other; inequality increases within the less numerous class in the same ratio in which it decreases in the community. Hence it would appear, on searching to the bottom, that aristocracy should naturally spring from the bosom of democracy.

But this kind of aristocracy in no way resembles those that preceded it. It will be noticed at once that since it applies exclusively to manufactures and to some manufacturing callings, it is a monstrous exception in the general aspect of society. The small aristocratic societies formed by some manufacturers in the midst of the immense democracy of our age contain, like the great aristocratic societies of former ages, some men who are very opulent and a multitude who are wretchedly poor. The poor have few means of escaping from their condition and becoming rich; but the rich are constantly becoming poor, or they give up business once they have made a fortune. Thus the elements of which the class of the poor is composed are fixed; but the elements of which the class of the rich is composed are not. To tell the truth, though there are rich men, the class of rich men does not exist. These rich individuals have no feelings or purposes in common, no shared traditions, no shared hopes. There are therefore members, but no body.

Not only are the rich not tightly united among themselves, but there is no real bond between them and the poor. Their relative position is not a permanent one; they are constantly drawn together or separated by their interests. The workman is generally dependent on the master, but not on any particular master. These two men meet in the factory, but do not know each other elsewhere; and while they come into contact on one point, they stand very wide apart on all others. The manufacturer asks nothing of the workman but his labor; the workman expects nothing from him but his wages. The one takes on no obligation to protect, nor the other to defend; they are not permanently connected by habit or by duty. The aristocracy created by business rarely settles in the midst of the manufacturing population it directs; the object is not to govern that population, but to use it. An aristocracy constituted in this way can have no great hold on those it employs, and even if it manages to keep them at one moment, they escape the next. It does not know how to will, and it cannot act. The territorial aristocracy of former ages was either bound by law, or thought itself bound by custom, to come to the relief of its serving men, and to help them in their distresses. But the manufacturing aristocracy of our age first impoverishes and debases the men who serve it, and then abandons them to be supported by the charity of the public. This is a natural consequence of what has been said before. Between the workmen and the master there are frequent relations, but no real partnership.

I am of the opinion, on the whole, that the manufacturing aristocracy now growing up under our eyes is one of the harshest that ever existed in the world; but at the same time it is one of the most confined and least dangerous. Nevertheless, the friends of democracy should keep their eyes anxiously fixed in this direction. For if ever a permanent inequality of conditions and aristocracy again penetrate the world, it can be predicted that this is the channel by which they will enter.
